transcript.answer: Otto uses one server-side key because the delivered OLT TMS External API only supports that. It authenticates every request with a single global `x-api-key` header. It has no user login, no OAuth flow, no login endpoint and no per-user credential. ADR-001 therefore rejected Option A, where each user forwards their own TMS token, because there is no user credential to forward. It also rejected Option B, where re:cinq exchanges or holds a per-user credential, because no such credential exists to exchange. Option C is the only one the API supports. It means a server-held key, with the boundary between customers enforced in Otto's own code. The key is company-scoped, not user-scoped, so it is the same for every user in the company. The requirement that customers can only see their own bookings is therefore enforced by Otto. Clerk authenticates the user, and the Clerk organisation carries the TMS `customerNumber`. A scope resolver (`apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts`) derives that `customerNumber` from the authenticated company, never from the model or the request. Every tool reaches the TMS client through the resolver.

judgements.reason: The answer says Otto uses a single global server-held key, with the customer boundary enforced in Otto's own code, because the TMS has no user-level auth or per-user credential to forward or exchange; this matches the gold, though it says 'company-scoped' where the gold says one key per integration partner.

The answer correctly says the TMS has no user-level auth, so forwarding is impossible, and that Otto enforces the customer boundary in its own code with one global key; it omits that the TMS issues one key per integration partner, saying only that the key is 'company-scoped'.
